Eternal Inheritance
ih-TUR-nul in-HAIR-ih-tunts
n. (eschatological promise)
From Latin aeternalis (eternal, from aetas, age) and hereditas (inheritance, from heres, heir); translating Greek tēn aiōnion klēronomian in Hebrews 9:15 — the klēros (lot, portion, allotted share) that belongs to the aiōn (the age to come, eternity). In the Old Testament background, the land of Canaan was Israel's inheritance (nachalâh); the eternal inheritance is its eschatological antitype.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The eternal inheritance is the eschatological portion promised to those who have been called through the mediation of Christ — the imperishable, undefiled, and unfading possession that awaits the redeemed in the fullness of the age to come. Hebrews 9:15 anchors the phrase in the new covenant: “He is the mediator of a new covenant — so that, since a death has taken place for the redemption of the transgressions that were committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.” The death of the testator is what activates the covenant-will: Christ died so that the inheritance He bequeathed could be legally transferred to His heirs. First Peter 1:4 fills in the character of what has been secured: “an inheritance imperishable, undefiled, and unfading — kept in heaven for you.” Three Greek alpha-privatives (without perishing, without defilement, without fading) describe an inheritance that is the negation of everything that can be taken, soiled, or diminished in this present age. Galatians 3:18 roots the inheritance in promise rather than Law: God granted it to Abraham by promise, not by legal performance, establishing that the eternal inheritance has always been a gift of grace to those who believe. Colossians 3:24 makes the inheritance the motivational ground of Christian service: “knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance. It is the Lord Christ whom you serve.” The inheritance is not earned by earthly labour; it is the reward given by the Lord Himself to those who serve Him faithfully, the final resolution of everything the saints have hoped for, worked toward, and suffered to obtain.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines inheritance as property or estate descending by law or custom from a parent or ancestor; in theology, the eternal inheritance is the eschatological estate bequeathed to God's adopted children through Christ's atoning death — imperishable, heavenly, and secured by the faithfulness of the divine Testator.

expand to see more

INHERITANCE, n. [L. hereditas.] An estate derived from an ancestor or, by extension, any possession received as a right or by divine gift. Webster (1828) distinguishes inheritance from a mere bequest: an inheritance belongs to the heir by virtue of the relationship, not only by the will's enactment.

The eternal inheritance in Scripture takes the Israelite land-grant tradition (Canaan as the inheritance of God's people) and elevates it to its eschatological antitype: a heavenly country (Heb 11:14–16) that is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Pet 1:4). What Canaan was typologically — God's people dwelling in God's land under God's rule — the eternal inheritance is antitypically and permanently.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 9:15 — "And for this reason He is the mediator of a new covenant — so that, since a death has taken place for the redemption of the transgressions that were committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance."

1 Peter 1:4 — "to an inheritance imperishable, undefiled, and unfading — kept in heaven for you,"

Colossians 3:24 — "knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance. It is the Lord Christ whom you serve."

Galatians 3:18 — "For if the inheritance is based on the Law, it is no longer based on a promise — but God has granted it to Abraham by means of a promise."

Modern Corruption

Prosperity theology turns the eternal inheritance into a present-age financial portfolio; dispensational theology over-specialises the inheritance as a Jewish land-promise rather than the universal eschatological estate of all who are Abraham's children by faith; therapeutic culture replaces the heavenly inheritance with self-actualisation as the ultimate telos.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel re-reads the inheritance promises of Scripture as entitlements to material wealth, health, and social prominence in this present age. The three alpha-privatives of 1 Pet 1:4 — imperishable, undefiled, unfading — deliberately describe what no earthly possession can be. The inheritance is defined by its difference from every earthly asset. To preach material prosperity as the inheritance is to take the one possession that moths and rust cannot destroy and replace it with the possessions moths and rust do destroy. Christ's own warning in Matt 6:19–21 is the direct counter.

Dispensationalism tends to partition the inheritance: the land promise belongs to national Israel in the millennium, and heaven belongs to the church. But Galatians 3:18–29 makes the inheritance available to all who are “in Christ Jesus” and therefore “Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise.” The eternal inheritance is not a Jewish entitlement re-distributed but the one eschatological estate inherited by all who are united to the Mediator by faith. The new heavens and new earth are not a dispensational consolation prize; they are the antitype of Canaan, the true rest (Heb 4:9) that the land of promise always pointed toward.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The eternal inheritance is the eschatological fulfilment of the patriarchal land-promise, the priestly inheritance in God Himself (Num 18:20), and the adoption into God's family that makes believers co-heirs with Christ (Rom 8:17) — the entire biblical inheritance theology condensed into one imperishable, heavenly estate.

expand to see more

Hebrew nachalâh — inheritance, portion; used of the land of Canaan as Israel's covenantal portion (Deut 4:21) and of God Himself as the Levites' inheritance (Num 18:20).

Greek klēronomia — inheritance; from klēros (lot, allotted portion) and nemo (to distribute); the eschatological portion allotted to the heirs of God.

Greek aiōnios — eternal, belonging to the age to come; the adjective that transforms the inheritance from temporal to eschatological in Heb 9:15.

Romans 8:17 — “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ”; the eternal inheritance belongs to those adopted as sons, co-inheritors with the firstborn Son who secured it by His death.

Hebrews 11:14–16 — the patriarchs “desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one”; their entire pilgrimage is interpreted as a forward-looking hope for the eternal inheritance that the land of Canaan typified.

Usage

"Hebrews 9:15 makes the death of Christ the legal event that activates the eternal inheritance: as the death of a testator enacts a will, Christ's death ratified the new covenant and released the inheritance promised to all who have been called."

"The three alpha-privatives of 1 Pet 1:4 — “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” — define the inheritance negatively as everything earthly possession cannot be, pointing the persecuted believer away from what can be taken and toward what can never be lost."

"Colossians 3:24 deploys the eternal inheritance as the motive for present-day faithful service: even unpaid, unrecognised, or enslaved labour done “as to the Lord” will be recompensed by the Lord Himself with the reward of the inheritance."
